Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg, EDSA corner Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City LEGAL SERVICE NOV 22 2010 DILG LEGAL OPINION NO. 145 s. 2010 HON. HAROUN ALRASHID A. LUCMAN, JR. DILG-ARMM Regional Secretary and Provincial Director Province of Lanao, Amai-Pakpak Brgy. Green, Marawi City Dear Regional Secretary Lucman, Jr.: This has reference to your letter seeking legal opinion on "whether the holdover term constitutes as ONE TERM in counting the three (3) consecutive terms ofa Barangay Chairman". In your letter, you cited two (2) scenarios and further stated that the opinion is much sought to help the DILG Provincial Office settle the issue pertaining thereto. Please take note that Scenario No. I is incomplete. Hence, may we be provided with the pertinent data which were not so provided in your letter in order for us to properly advise you on the matter. RA 91641, as amended by RA 9340, fixed the date of the barangay and SK elections, prescribed the term of office of the barangay and SK officials, and provided for the qualifications of candidates and voters for the SK elections. The word "term" in a legal sense means a fixed and definite period of time which the law describes that an officer may hold an office. According to Mechem, the term of office is the period during which an office may be held. Upon expiration of the officer's term, unless he is authorized by law to HOLDOVER, his rights, duties and authority as a public officer must ipso facto cease. In the law of public officers, the most and natural frequent method by which a public officer ceases to be such is by the expiration of the terms for which he was elected or appointed. A later case, Gaminde v. Commission on Audit, reiterated that "[T]he term means the time during which the officer may claim to bold Office as of right, and fixes the interval after which the several incumbents shall succeed one another. "2 The application of the holdover principle as provided for in Section 5 of RA 9164 preserves continuity in the transaction of official business and prevents a hiatus in government pending the assumption of a successor into office. 1 An Act Providing For Synchronized Barangay And Sangguniang Kabataan Elections, Amending Republic Act No. 7160, As Amended, Otherwise Known As The "Local Government Code Of 1991", And For Other Purposes 2 Aldovino vs Commission On Elections, G.R. No. 184836, 23 December 2009

prevents a hiatus in government pending the assumption of a successor into office. Ergo, the holdover period does not constitute a separate term but merely a valid extension period during which an incumbent may legally perform the functions of his office pending the assumption of a successor. Delving on the scenarios you presented, we tackle Scenario 2 whereby a S- termer Punong Barangay (Dan Salcedo) runs for the position of a 'Kagavyad' while his son (Ronnie Salcedo) runs for the post of a Punong Barangay, and after being elected as such, the son relinquishes his post as Punong Barangay to give way to his successor, presumably the father, being the highest ranking sanggunian barangay member. Under this premise, we can only substantiate the issue on a valid succession as sanctioned by Section 44 (b) of the Local Government Code of 1991, wherein the highest ranking sanggunian member becomes the Punong Barangay in case a permanent vacancy occurs in the latter post, as mentioned in your Scenario 2. The issue as to whether the acts of the father and son constitute a "circumvention of law" is not for this Department to determine. A person aggrieved by acts perceived to be contrary to law, such as in the given case where the alleged assumption to office appears to be a circumvention of the law, may file a petition before the Regional Trial Court to question the said assumption to office. We hope that the foregoing sufficiently resolves your concerns. Very truly yours, ATTY. JES Director III LS:55/rb B. DO
